utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor against Slobodan Miljkovic, alias Lugar; Blagoje Simic; Milan Simic; Miroslav Tadic, alias Miro Brko; Stevan Todorovic, alias Stiv, alias Stevo, alias Monstrum; Simo Zaric, alias Solaja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Registrar, can we have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, for the time being, I'm going to ask you to be seated or, perhaps, it would be best to give Mr. Todorovic his headphones. Do you hear me, Mr. Todorovic? This is the Presiding Judge speaking to you. Please state your name, your first name, your profession, your age, and the domicile that you had before your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: My name is Stevan Todorovic. I was born 29 December, 1957 in Bosanski Samac. My address is in Donja Slatina, Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Your profession, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am an engineer of machinery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. I would like the representatives of the two parties to identify themselves. First of all, turning to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues Ms. Paterson, Mr. Michelich, and Ms. Annink for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am Goran Neskovic from Doboj in the Republika Srpska. I have been assigned as counsel for Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is Mr. Neskovic registered in the bar and has he given all the official documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. He has been assigned officially by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you speak one of the two official languages of the Tribunal, Mr. Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not speak one of the two official languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which languages do you speak? Perhaps I misunderstood the interpretation. The interpreters said you didn't speak one of the two languages. I understood that you did speak one of them, one of the two, that is. You do not speak either of the languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I do not speak either of the two official languages of the Tribunal, neither English nor French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, neither of the two. The registrar has placed your name on our list. I make no comments, other than to say to you that this may sometimes cause, not problems, specifically related to your client, because he has a lawyer with whom he can understand things and with whom he gets along with well. But there are frequently motions and briefs that are filed with this Tribunal, if only by the other party. They are going to come, and they will be presented, so that you understand this is a French speaking Trial Chamber. But this is something you already know. We are here for the initial appearance of Mr. Todorovic. Let me remind you that Mr. Todorovic was included in an indictment which was confirmed in 1995, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. It was confirmed on the 21st of July, 1995 by Judge Vohrah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will come back to this because there are other accused already in the United Nations detention facility in The Hague. Mr. Todorovic, today this is your initial appearance. You are going to, after certain text are read, you are going to state before the Tribunal in respect of the various charges which the Prosecutor has brought against you and which were confirmed in 1995 by a judge, you will plead either guilty or not guilty to each of the counts. After this we will attempt to see how we can organise the rest of the proceedings with the difficulty, of course, that in this Tribunal now, we are going through all kinds of preparatory phases that were specifically carried out in relation to this specific indictment and which involve three other accused who are, today, being held in the detention unit. Without any further adieu, perhaps we could turn to the registrar and ask the registrar to read the relevant articles in the indictment. Perhaps Mr. Neskovic would care to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I have not been asked whether we had prepared for the initial appearance. You realise that I arrived here yesterday. I talked to Mr. Stevan Todorovic. However, I was not able to reach -- I was not able to discuss things with him because of his health conditions. During the process of his arrest in the former Yugoslavia, he received a very heavy blow with a baseball bat over his head. I requested of Mr. Jean-Jacques Heintz yesterday to have an MRI. This has not been done so far. Some injuries may only appear within seven days, a certain hematoma. Mr. Todorovic has complained of headaches and nausea and all day yesterday, and I believe that it would not be appropriate for him to go through the initial appearance today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First, we're going to ask Mr. Todorovic's opinion, and then I would like to hear comments from the Office of the Prosecutor, and I will also, of course, hear what my colleagues have to say. Mr. Todorovic, will you please stand? You are before an International Tribunal. You may have full confidence in this Tribunal and say what you wish to say at this moment, and then we will see what has to be done. Mr. Todorovic, how do you feel? First of all, would you prefer to speak while seated, because your lawyer has drawn a rather negative picture of your medical condition, or would you prefer to speak while you are still standing up?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may sit down, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. You may, of course, speak sitting down, Mr. Todorovic. Would you explain or, first, tell us, please, how you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't feel well, because during the kidnapping, I was transported from Serbia by boat, and I received a heavy blow with a baseball bat over my head. I still feel a headache, dizziness, nausea, and I have occasional vomiting. As Attorney Neskovic said, I had a visit by the medical doctor, and this was just a superficial examination without any x-ray or any MRI. My apologies. I still have a scar here in the back of my head that is a laceration. There may be a hematoma underneath, and if I have any abrupt movements, and if I lean back onto the cushion, I get a feeling of dizziness and nausea and I vomit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask the Registrar, since we spoke with Mr. Jean-Jacques Heintz, I suppose that these examinations have been scheduled? Is that correct, Mr. Registrar? Would you speak on behalf of the registry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Heintz is aware of this request and I'm sure that the MRI will not be postponed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to give the floor to the Office of the Prosecutor and then turn to Mr. Neskovic. We have tried to apply the rules in the most flexible way possible. I can recall that Rule 62, as in all legal systems, states that when there is an arrest, there must be an appearance quickly before a judge, and perhaps, Mr. Neskovic, if we had not had Mr. Todorovic appear today, would now be preparing a motion in which he would state that it was not normal for his client to be thrown into the detention unit in Scheveningen without having seen a judge. Therefore, I think his rights have been explained to the client, but I would like to hear what he has to say. This was not an order to try to surprise you. Mr. Todorovic was arrested when, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic arrived in the detention unit on Sunday, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sunday. All right. Today is Wednesday. It doesn't seem particularly strange to me for there to be two or three days to go by before the initial appearance. It's the time necessary for Mr. Todorovic to know how the proceedings are conducted. We will see whether if it is possible to continue or not. Let me now turn to Mr. Niemann or to one of the other representatives of the OTP and ask what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Unfortunately, Your Honours, we're not in a position to assist the Trial Chamber with any of the details of the arrest. We don't know what details occurred there. With respect to the situation we find ourselves in now, the position of the Prosecution is that we would be reluctant to see a plea taken from the accused, be it guilty or not guilty, if he has said directly and through his counsel that he is not well. Our concern would be that if he is not well, he is probably not in the best position to indicate to the Court his attitude to the charges that are laid against him. Your Honours are rightfully concerned about the issue of an accused being put in detention and not being brought before a judge as expeditiously as possible, and that, of course, is an issue that the Prosecution shares with Your Honours. In our submission, Your Honours, two of the very important components of Rule 62 can be properly satisfied at this stage without the necessity of taking a plea. Firstly, Your Honours need satisfy yourselves that the accused is properly represented by counsel. Your Honours can satisfy yourselves of that fact because counsel does appear here today in respect of Mr. Todorovic and has made submissions on his behalf. With respect to reading in the indictment, which is also an important matter, we would submit, Your Honours, if counsel for Mr. Todorovic were to give you an undertaking to read the indictment to him at the very earliest possible time, Your Honours could be satisfied that he has had read to him the indictment in a language that he understands. If counsel for the Defence were prepared to give that undertaking to Your Honours at this stage, then two of the concerns that are dealt with in Rule 62 would be, in my respectful submission, disposed of. That wouldn't preclude, Your Honours, a formal procedure of coming before the Chamber at a time when the accused is in better medical condition and for the formal procedure of reading the indictment and taking charges to take place. There are two issues. One is for the Court to ascertain the attitude of the accused to the indictment, which is dealt with in subparagraph 3 of Rule 62, and there is another issue, and that is Your Honours being satisfied that the accused is aware of the charges against to him. That can be done in another way, which is to obtain an undertaking from counsel for the Defence, that at the very earliest possible opportunity he will make sure that the accused is fully acquainted with the terms of the indictment. Then, of course, Your Honours, if the case was to be adjourned on the basis that it can be brought on at any time before Your Honours, subject to Your Honours' convenience, at short notice, then any concerns that the accused may have about being incarcerated before a formal plea has been taken can be resolved by that process. Then we can only hope that the medical condition of the accused improves rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. There are two concepts here. Mr. Todorovic or at least his counsel have understood, first was the requirement that an accused cannot remain in an indictment before a Trial Chamber in a court, especially an international court. We have to keep in mind the concept of human rights, but he cannot remain in a detention facility either without having had an initial appearance, which is what we're doing today. What the Prosecutor has just raised, Mr. Neskovic, is that, in fact, we might postpone the guilty pleas, but I do point out that if you have read the indictment, the accused can make no plea at all, if he so chooses, and at that point all his rights are guaranteed. Let me look at Rule 62(3), which is: We call upon the accused to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on each count, should the accused fail to do so, enter a plea of not guilty on the accused's behalf, which does not preclude if, subsequently, he would like to plead not guilty. We have already had examples of similar cases in other cases with which this Trial Chamber is familiar. A third point: The Prosecutor has, in a sense, sent you back the ball. You have to know what it is that you want, Mr. Neskovic. The Judges here are very attentive to what you wish, but I think that you must speak with your client about this. We, here, cannot take an opinion from Mr. Todorovic because he doesn't feel good. We are not in a tremendous hurry to have this initial appearance, but my colleagues and myself wanted to see Mr. Todorovic today. Nonetheless, the Prosecutor has provided an opening, and he has asked that not only one of the provisions of the text which has already been carried out, is that you introduce yourself, but that you would read or have the indictment read to the accused. He was already read the indictment when he was arrested. Before I give the floor back to you, Mr. Neskovic, I would like to turn to Mr. Todorovic. I ask him to remain seated. At the time of your arrest, did they read the indictment to you? Please remain seated. Did they read the indictment to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Since I was in very bad shape, they were showing me something, but I do not know what specifically. I do not know what they were reading to me. There were some papers there, but there was -- even there was something on one page, but I don't know exactly what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. We can consider that at the time of your arrest you were not conscious of what was being read to you. Let me now turn to Mr. Neskovic. Since the arrest and since you have been working on this case, did you have the opportunity of reading, as you must do according to the rules of the Tribunal, did you read the indictment to the accused and what impressions did you get from him? You must have felt something while you were reading it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have not at all examined the indictment with my client, nor have I discussed it with him. My first contact with him was yesterday, and we spent the whole time discussing his health. Please do not take me wrong. The initial appearance could take place tomorrow after a scan is taken of his head. I have said this out of caution, and the practice in this Tribunal so far has shown that if the defendant doesn't feel well, we must request a full medical examination so that we know that he's fully conscious of where he is or what the indictment says and that he may enter a proper plea. I have not asked for any adjournment. I have just familiarised you with his state of health. I found him in his pyjamas, the pyjamas he was wearing when he was taken into custody in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I cannot go into the details of the procedure of his arrest. The Tribunal could request such information from the appropriate unit of the SFOR. All that I'm asking is that a scan be taken of his head to make sure that there is no hematoma inside, and then we can have an initial appearance, if necessary, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, your request is actually official. I would like your request to be made official, that you would like this appearance to be postponed. We want to be very clear here and understand one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm proposing that we postpone the initial appearance because of the medical condition of Mr. Todorovic, but in order to assist the Trial Chamber, I propose that we have the initial appearance as early as tomorrow, if the examination is carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You heard the request of the Defence who prefers that this initial appearance take place only after the MRI, if, in fact, the Registrar orders that one should be done. Do you agree with that, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We agree with that. We think that's a sensible course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleagues. Mr. Todorovic, please remain seated, Mr. Neskovic, as well. First of all, Mr. Todorovic, from the Registrar, we have just received certain information about your medical condition. Do you agree, since the registry did do something, and this is a public hearing, the registry has not ignored the situation, has not paid attention to it? Do you agree that I reveal what was done? Do you agree to my explaining what your medical condition is as of today, once the formalities that were taken by the registry were carried out? Would you like to speak on behalf of your client, Mr. Neskovic? I'm also going to ask your client. In other words, what I want to say in public is that everything that was possible to do was done when Mr. Todorovic arrived. Perhaps there are other things that can be done, we haven't got to that point yet. For the time being, there are formalities that were carried out after Mr. Todorovic, after his arrest. First, I would like to ask that you agree to my revealing what was done. Mr. Todorovic, do you agree to my revealing these things?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must say that I was given some medical attention, but a visual examination cannot disclose whether there is anything behind those outside injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's not the question I'm asking. I'm simply asking whether you agree to my revealing what was done by the efforts of the registry on the medical level. Do you agree or do you not agree to my stating what was done? Your counsel said yes, but I would like to have your opinion, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is not a great secret. I would simply like to point out that the accused was seen by the physician at the detention unit, who called in a neurologist for consultation, who made a diagnosis of a hematoma and said that an MRI, at this point, was not necessary. I'm not saying that one should not be done. I'm not a physician. I simply wanted to make this clarification to the public, but with your authorisation. Having made this clarification, the question which the Judges must now respond to is whether or not to continue with this initial appearance. We would like to ask Mr. Todorovic and his counsel, are you, at least, in a condition to hear the reading of the indictment? We're not going to ask you to plead guilty or not guilty. We will simply note that you have entered a plea of not guilty. Are you in a condition which would allow you to hear the reading of this indictment? Since your counsel has not had the opportunity to read it to you. Take your time, you may consult with one another. If you want to consult with your client, Mr. Neskovic, and you can do it in private, if you care to. Mr. Todorovic, are you in a condition to hear the indictment and then we will enter a plea of not guilty, I'm not going to ask you to do what we do with all of the accused, that is, to rise, but simply in public, we will replace the reading of the indictment, which should have been done to you, had you been in better condition yesterday. Do you agree that we read it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there may be a break so that I may consult with my counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will suspend the hearing for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Please be seated. Mr. Todorovic, we have given you as much time as you needed in order to consult with your counsel. We thought that we would read the indictment. What is your opinion? After you have spoken with Mr. Neskovic, your counsel, what is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to thank you for giving me this opportunity to consult with my counsel. I informed you yesterday in writing that I'm not feeling well. I hope you received that letter. I do not feel capable of following the reading of the indictment. If counsel could read it to me when I am in a better condition, because I would like to lie down awhile, because I still am feeling pain and dizziness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to consult with my colleagues. The Tribunal has noted your opinion, Mr. Todorovic, but in view of everything that was revealed having to do with your medical condition, also with your approval, and since it is your right, we're not going to ask you to plead guilty or not guilty. Since you're tired, we can do that another time. However, since this is a public hearing, we are going to read the indictment, that is, the relevant parts that concern you, and then we will adjourn for another initial appearance when the Tribunal will know that the indictment has been read, which is a basic document, and you must have heard it. Because, apparently, we were not able to give it to you before that. Therefore, I will now ask the Registrar to read the relevant parts. We're only going to read those relevant parts of the indictment that deal with you, and then we will adjourn. You will provisionally be noted as having pled not guilty, and then we will have a further initial appearance in which, once you are completely better, you will be able to express an opinion as to each of the charges. Registrar, read the general parts of the indictment and then only the relevant part which has to do with Mr. Todorovic. If you don't feel well, Mr. Todorovic, you will ask the reading to be interrupted, although we do hope that it can be read until the end.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Slobodan Miljkovic, alias Lugar; Blagoje Simic; Milan Simic; Miroslav Tadic, alias Miro Brko; Stevan Todorovic, alias Stiv, alias Stevo, alias Monstrum; Simo Zaric, alias Solaja. As regards Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, and Miroslav Tadic, they are part of a new indictment which was confirmed on the 25th of August and whose initial appearance already took place on the 3rd of September, 1998. Indictment: Richard J. Goldstone, Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to his authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (Tribunal Statute) charges: 1) In 1991, almost 17.000 Bosnian Croats and Muslims, of a total population of about 33.000, lived in the municipality of Bosanski Samac in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. By May 1995, fewer than 300 of the Bosnian Croat and Muslim residents remained. 2) On 17 April, 1992, Serb military forces from Bosnia and elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia seized control of the town of Bosanski Samac. 3) Because of its location at the northwestern edge of the Posavina Corridor, control of Bosanski Samac was important to Serb efforts to create a Serb-controlled land bridge between Serbia and the Krajina Serbs in Croatia and western Bosnia and Herzegovina. 4) After seizing control in the military takeover, Serb authorities undertook a campaign of terror designed to force most Bosnian Croat and Muslim residents to leave the area. 5) Beginning on 17 April, 1992, Serb military and political authorities coordinated and carried out the following actions as part of that campaign of terror: a) arrested and detained most of the Bosnian Croat and Muslim men in the municipality, particularly the political, economic, professional, academic, and civic leaders; b) established and operated, primarily under the authority of the Serb police, detention camps where prisoners were killed, beaten, tortured, sexually assaulted, and otherwise mistreated; c) permitted units of paramilitary soldiers from Serbia to enter the detention camps to kill and beat the prisoners; d) forced Bosnian Croat and Muslim residents to leave their homes and permitted Serb residents to move into the vacated houses; e) expelled, through force or intimidation, Bosnian Croat and Muslim residents of the municipality to other countries and other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina; f) required Bosnian Croat and Muslim men, women, and children to work on forced labour projects, such as digging trenches and other work at military confrontation lines; g) robbed Bosnian Croat and Muslim residents of their cars, cash and valuables, and looted their homes; h) looted and dismantled equipment and inventories from Bosnian Croat and Muslim businesses; i) issued orders prohibiting Bosnian Croats and Muslims from congregating in public and requiring Bosnian Croats and Muslims to wear white arm bands to identify themselves as non-Serbs; j) confiscated the bank accounts of many Bosnian Croats and Muslims and blocked the funds in those accounts; k) mobilised Bosnian Croat and Muslim men into the Bosnian Serb army and sent them to the frontlines; i) created such an atmosphere of fear and oppression among the non-Serb population that most Bosnian Croat and Muslim residents fled the area. The accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go directly to this accused.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Accused: 10) Stevan Todorovic, also known as Stiv, Stevo, or Monstrum, born in 1957, from Donja Slatina, Bosanski Samac municipality, was appointed Chief of Police for Bosanski Samac after the 17 April, 1992 military takeover. Before then, Stevan Todorovic was an executive in a bamboo furniture factory. General allegations: 12) Unless otherwise set forth below, all acts and omissions alleged in this indictment took place between about 17 April and 20 November, 1992 in the Bosanski Samac municipality in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. 13) At all times relevant to this indictment, a state of armed conflict and partial occupation existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 14) At all times relevant to this indictment, all persons described in this indictment as victims were protected by the Geneva Conventions of 1949. 15) At all times relevant to this indictment, all of the accused in this indictment were required to abide by the laws and customs governing the conduct of war, including the Geneva Conventions of 1949. 16) In each paragraph of this indictment charging torture, the acts were committed by, or at the instigation of, or with the consent or acquiescence of, an official or person acting in an official capacity, and for one or more of the following purposes: To obtain information or a confession from the victim or a third person; to punish the victim for an act the victim or a third person committed or was suspected of having committed; to intimidate or coerce the victim or a third person; and/or for any reason based upon discrimination of any kind. 17) All acts and omissions charged as crimes against humanity were part of a widespread, systematic, or large-scale attack against the Croat and Muslim residents of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. 18) Each of the accused is individually responsible for the crimes alleged against him in this indictment, pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Tribunal Statute. Individual criminal liability includes committing, planning, initiating, ordering, or aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or execution of any crime referred to in Articles 2 to 5 of the Tribunal Statute. 19) Paragraphs 12 through 18 are realleged and incorporated into each of the charges set forth below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, leave out the counts that do not directly affect the accused, except those that affect him indirectly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Counts 27 to 29: Killing of Anto Brandic: 28) On about 29 July, 1992, in the hallway of the SUP building in Bosanski Samac, Stevan Todorovic and others killed Anto Brandic, also known as Antesa, by repeatedly beating and kicking him with police batons and heavy boots. By these actions, Stevan Todorovic committed or otherwise aided and abetted: Count 27: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(a) (willful killing) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 28: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 29: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 30 to 32: Beatings in the SUP Building: 29) On about 29 July, 1992, in the hallway of the SUP building in Bosanski Samac, Stevan Todorovic and others repeatedly beat and kicked Enver Ibralic, Hasan Jasarevic, Omer Nalic, and Father Jozo Puskaric with police batons and heavy boots, thereby causing the victims physical injury. By these actions, Stevan Todorovic committed or otherwise aided and abetted: Count 30: a grave breach (willfully causing great suffering) recognised by the Article 2(c) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 31: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by the Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 32: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i) (inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 33 to 35: Beating of Silvestar Antunovic: 30) On about 15 July, 1992, in the gymnasium of the Bosanski Samac primary school, Stevan Todorovic and others repeatedly beat Silvestar Antunovic with a large wooden club. As a result of the beating, Silvestar Antunovic suffered partial paralysis and other serious physical injury. By these actions, Stevan Todorovic committed or otherwise aided and abetted: Count 33: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(c) (willfully causing great suffering) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 34: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 35: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i) (inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 36 to 38: Sexual Assault: 31) On about 13 June, 1992 in the hallway of the Bosanski Samac SUP building, Stevan Todorovic forced Witness A and Witness B to perform sexual acts upon each other in the presence of several other prisoners and guards. By these actions, Stevan Todorovic instigated, ordered, and committed: Count 36: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(b) (inhumane treatment) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 37: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(c) (humiliating and degrading treatment) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 38: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(g) (rape, which includes other forms of sexual assault) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 39 to 41: Torture of Omer Nalic: 32) On about 19 June, 1992 at the Bosanski Samac primary school, while questioning Omer Nalic about a radio transmitter, Stevan Todorovic ordered three men to beat Omer Nalic. By these actions, Stevan Todorovic instigated, ordered, committed or aided and abetted: Count 39: a grave breach recognised by Article 2(b) (torture) of the Tribunal Statute; Count 40: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (torture) of the Geneva Conventions; Count 41: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(f) (torture) of the Tribunal Statute. Counts 42 to 56 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Registrar. These counts do not directly affect your client, Mr. Neskovic, but I would like paragraphs 33 and 34 to be read, because the Prosecutor is alleging certain links of authority and, at this stage, they should be read. Mr. Registrar, do not read 42 to 56, but only paragraphs 33 and 34 for the benefit of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 33) After about 17 April 1992, Blagoje Simic was the highest ranking civilian official in the municipality of Bosanski Samac and, as such, was in a position of superior authority to Stevan Todorovic, the newly-appointed Serb Chief of Police. 34) With respect to the acts and omissions of Stevan Todorovic set forth in this indictment, Blagoje Simic knew or had reason to know that Stevan Todorovic was about to commit such acts or had done so, and Blagoje Simic failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish Stevan Todorovic. By these acts or omissions, Blagoje Simic was criminally responsible for the actions of Stevan Todorovic. This is an indictment signed by Richard Goldstone on the 21st of June, 1995 and confirmed by Judge Vohrah on the 25th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic and Mr. Todorovic, we are now going to adjourn. The Tribunal is now assured that the reading that should have been done in the previous days has been done. The initial appearance, at which your client will be called upon to plead guilty or not guilty, after the possible medical treatment which will be arranged by the registry, when your client will be capable of pleading guilty or not guilty on each count, in principle, we will not be rereading the indictment, except if Mr. Todorovic wishes the indictment to be reread. For the moment, Mr. Registrar, I would like it to be noted that, at the present stage, Mr. Todorovic pleads not guilty, but it should also be recorded that he wanted to abstain, but this is for the full implementation of the relevant Articles of the Rules of Procedures and Evidence. We will be hearing Mr. Todorovic's plea after consulting with his Defence counsel, and then we will organise the continuation of the proceedings, taking into account what has already been done. In this particular case, the three other accused that are in detention in the detention unit in Scheveningen, I wish to remind you that I have already appointed a Pre-Trial Judge, which will be Judge Rodrigues. According to the new rules, this instance will ensure the more expeditious preparation of trial. We will, of course, organise all the other dates and schedules regarding disclosure and everything else. We would have had a Status Conference today concerning Simic, Tadic, Zaric but, in agreement with Judge Rodrigues and Judge Riad, we preferred to postpone that Status Conference until after the initial appearance of the new accused, who is here present, Mr. Todorovic. Before closing, I turn to Mr. Neskovic. Have you any comments to make regarding what has been said or anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NESKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the present, I have no questions. I see that you have taken note of everything that we have said so far, and I hope that Mr. Todorovic will be able to plead the next time when his condition improves. In view of the fact that you've mentioned the other three accused linked to this indictment, I hope that the schedule of trial will not affect the quality of the defence of Mr. Todorovic, that is, that he will have sufficient time to prepare his defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, I should like to give you the floor last. I hope you're not feeling too unwell. You will be taken care of by the doctors. Have you anything to add to this Trial Chamber and to what has been said by your counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have nothing to add. I wish to thank you for your understanding about my condition, and I hope that it will improve after medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, the hearing is adjourned. A date will be set in accordance with the Prosecutor, the Defence counsel, and the state of health of the accused. The registry will notify us, all of us, of that new initial appearance. The hearing is adjourned.
